content: 1. Mobile clinics, outreach teams, and community support groups are examples of community-based services that provide healthcare access to populations in need. 2. Cities and other administrative regions of epidemiological importance are often targeted for healthcare interventions. 3. The percentage of opioid-dependent individuals receiving opioid agonist maintenance treatment (OAMT) on a specified date measures the coverage of OAMT among this population. 4. This indicator can be measured at the level of service providers or at the population level. 5. OAMT is a critical component of harm reduction services as it directly reduces the number of injection-related risk acts among people who inject drugs. 6. The numerator is the number of individuals on OAMT at a specified census date. 7. The denominator varies: at the service provider level, it is the number of opioid-dependent individuals accessing the service; at the population level, it is the estimated size of the opioid-dependent population in the relevant geographic area. 8. Measurement is based on individual-level data obtained from program records. 9. The total population of opioid-dependent individuals includes both those who inject drugs and those who consume opioids through other routes. 10. Not all OAMT recipients have a history of injecting drugs, and not all people who inject drugs are dependent on opioids. 11. Data can be disaggregated by gender (female, male, or other), age (<25 years, 25+ years), provider type (key population-led, community-led, public sector, private for-profit, or not-for-profit organizations), and service setting (facility-based or community-based). 12. The percentage of person-years of follow-up (PYFU) on OAMT among opioid-dependent individuals measures the proportion of time individuals are covered by OAMT. 13. Evidence shows that HIV risk is reduced among opioid-dependent individuals during periods when they are receiving OAMT. 14. The numerator is the total PYFU on OAMT during a defined reporting period, calculated as the sum of the time on OAMT for each recipient during the reporting period. 15. The denominator varies: at the service provider level, it is the estimated PYFU for all opioid-dependent individuals accessing the service; at the population level, it is the estimated PYFU for the total opioid-dependent population in the relevant geographic area during the reporting period. 16. Data is obtained from individual-level program records and can be disaggregated by gender, age, provider type, and service setting. 17. The percentage of OAMT recipients who received treatment for at least six months measures retention in OAMT programs and the quality of treatment prescription. 18. Evidence indicates that the maximum benefit of OAMT is achieved when treatment lasts at least six months. 19. The numerator is the number of individuals in a cohort retained in OAMT for at least six months. 20. The denominator is the number of individuals starting OAMT during a defined cohort recruitment period. 21. Measurement is based on individual-level data obtained from program records and can be disaggregated by gender, age, provider type, and service setting. 22. The percentage of OAMT recipients receiving a maintenance dose greater than or equal to the recommended minimum dose measures the adequacy of OAMT dosing. 23. Evidence shows that the maximum benefit of OAMT is achieved when individuals receive at least the recommended minimum maintenance dose. 24. The numerator is the number of individuals, on a specified date, maintained on methadone or buprenorphine at the recommended minimum maintenance dose (≥60 mg of methadone or ≥8 mg of buprenorphine). 25. The denominator is the number of individuals receiving a maintenance dose of methadone or buprenorphine on a specified date, excluding those being inducted on OAMT or on reducing doses. 26. Measurement is based on individual-level data obtained from program records and can be disaggregated by gender, age, provider type, and service setting. 27. The total number of voluntary medical male circumcisions (VMMCs) performed according to national standards during the reporting period measures progress in scaling up male circumcision services. 28. WHO and UNAIDS recommend VMMC as an effective intervention for HIV prevention in priority countries and regions with high HIV prevalence and low male circumcision prevalence. 29. Randomized controlled trials have shown that VMMC performed by trained health professionals with proper equipment can reduce the risk of men acquiring HIV heterosexually. 30. The numerator is the total number of individuals undergoing VMMC performed according to national standards during the reporting period. 31. Measurement is based on individual-level data obtained from program records, such as VMMC registers, with a recommended reporting period of 12 months. 32. Data can be disaggregated by age, HIV status, provider type, and service setting. 33. The percentage of adverse events during the reporting period measures whether VMMC services meet national standards of safety and effectiveness. 34. Staff conducting medical circumcisions must have appropriate training and access to proper equipment. 35. Trends in adverse events may indicate areas where service providers need additional support. 36. Intraoperative adverse events may include pain, excessive bleeding, anesthesia-related effects, excessive skin removal, penile damage, or sharps injuries to personnel. 37. Postoperative adverse events may include abnormal pain, excessive swelling, infection, hematoma, bleeding, difficulty urinating, wound disruption, scarring, disfigurement, or injury to the glans. 38. Moderate or severe adverse events include complications resulting in death, hospitalization within 30 days, or permanent disability. 39. The numerator is the number of individuals experiencing at least one moderate or severe adverse event during or following circumcision surgery during the reporting period. 40. The denominator is the total number of individuals undergoing VMMC performed according to national standards during the reporting period. 41. Measurement is based on individual-level data obtained from program records and can be reported as the absolute number of adverse events or as a proportion of procedures conducted. 42. Data can be disaggregated by age, type and seriousness of adverse event, timing of adverse event (intraoperative or postoperative), service site, provider type, and service setting. 43. The percentage of people who used condoms with a non-regular partner in the last 12 months measures the extent of condom use among individuals at higher risk of HIV transmission. 44. Condom use during the last high-risk sexual act provides an indication of overall levels and trends of protected and unprotected sex. 45. Changes in condom use reflect community norms, condom availability, and individual motivation to protect themselves during sexual activity. 46. Quantifying the number of unprotected high-risk sexual acts is critical for modeling HIV transmission. 47. For men who have sex with men, the indicator measures the number of men reporting anal sex with a non-regular male partner in the last six months. 48. For transgender and gender-diverse individuals, the indicator measures the number reporting anal sex with a non-regular male partner in the last six months. 49. For people who inject drugs, the indicator measures the number reporting sex with a partner in the last month. 50. Countries may adjust the time period for defining key population groups based on the epidemic context or program focus. 51. Measurement for the general population is based on surveys such as the Demographic and Health Survey or AIDS Indicator Survey, while for key populations, it is based on representative surveys like bio-behavioral surveys. 52. Trends should be interpreted alongside changes in the percentage of individuals with multiple sexual partners or non-regular partners in the last 12 months, disaggregated by sex and age. 53. Data can be disaggregated by gender and age. 54. The number and percentage of people living with HIV who know their HIV status measures the extent of HIV testing and diagnosis. 55. Knowledge of HIV status is the entry point for treatment and care for people living with HIV and for prevention interventions for those at elevated risk of HIV acquisition. 56. Disaggregated estimates reveal gaps in access to testing among key groups of people living with HIV. 57. The numerator is the number of people living with HIV who have received their diagnosis and are still alive. 58. The denominator is the estimated number of people living with HIV. 59. Measurement for the numerator is based on the best estimate from available data sources, including HIV case surveillance systems.
